articles.title: Javier Milei's Pack of Giant Libertarian Dogs
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
There's an old saying about the loneliness of politics: If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog. The same may be true in Buenos Aires.
Argentine President Javier Milei is known for advocating economic liberty and classical liberal ideals. He regularly cites and quotes famous libertarian economists in speeches. And he has shrunk Argentina's bloated government, cutting spending and regulations in a bid to blunt the country's sky-high inflation. Judged strictly on that measure, his efforts have worked, cutting annual inflation from 211 percent down to 33 percent in less than three years. Milei is arguably the world's foremost elected advocate for, and implementer of, small government.
Although he likes his government small, he prefers his dogs very, very big.
Milei is reportedly the proud owner of five English mastiffs, an ancient British guard dog breed that commonly weighs in at more than 200 pounds.
After a surprising success in a 2023 presidential primary, Milei thanked his dogs, calling them his "four-legged children." But they're nobody's kids. His current gang of huge hounds consists entirely of clones of a single dog, Conan, named for the barbarian famously played onscreen by Arnold Schwarzenegger. After the original Conan passed away, Milei, who had previously banked the dog's genetic material, paid a reported $50,000 to have him cloned.
Dog-cloning procedures typically produce just one viable dog, but in this case the process produced at least five—by some reports six, one of whom apparently died young. (One report suggests only four dogs now remain, though this is unverified.)
In keeping with his free market philosophy, Milei named four of the dogs after a trio of libertarian economists: Murray, after Murray Rothbard; Milton, after Milton Friedman; and Robert and Lucas, after Robert Lucas Jr. A fifth dog is named Conan, after the original. Milei, who has no children, has said that the cloned Conan is "literally a son to me" and likened the other four to grandchildren.
It's not hard to see why a maximalist with libertarian tendencies like Milei might appreciate this specific breed of dog. English mastiffs are gentle giants, known for being calm and loyal but also watchful and vigilant. They are protectors of persons and property who can have a surprisingly fine-tuned sense of who is and isn't a threat, and where exactly the boundaries of one's lands begin and end. If the minarchist vision of the night-watchman state had an animal avatar, it would be the English mastiff.
English mastiffs are bodyguards and property managers. They are also pretty good friends and companions. That's clearly how Milei sees his dogs. Since his rise to political prominence, he has talked repeatedly about how the original Conan was his best friend, a comfort in times of loneliness who remained loyal and never left his side, even during difficult moments. Milei puts up with his pets' big-dog shenanigans, saying on television in 2018 that his "house is like Kosovo….In two weeks, they've eaten almost four armchairs." The largest of the dogs is 220 pounds.
Mastiffs are known for being strong-willed and sometimes stubborn-minded, partly because of breed personality and partly because of sheer size. Unlike many smaller dogs, which can be picked up or moved around by force, mastiffs can, in some sense, do whatever they want, because they have the ability to knock you over if they disagree. Every interaction with a mastiff is a negotiation, an exercise in convincing them to agree to your terms. Convincing a mastiff to sit, stay, lie down, and stop eating the couch is pretty good training for the back-and-forth exchange of a market economy.
In a profile of Milei's relationship with his dogs that this piece draws from, The New York Times noted that "Argentine news outlets have also reported that Mr. Milei has privately said that he has received strategic advice from his dogs." When asked, Milei did not flatly deny that he sometimes takes advice from his pets.
As the owner of two bullmastiffs (a similar though not quite as large breed of English giant made by combining the English mastiff with the English bulldog) I'll just say that this is not, perhaps, quite as strange as it sounds. Large dogs have humanlike qualities simply by virtue of their size; they weigh and take up as much space as a person. Mastiffs also have large eyes and short noses, giving them a more human appearance. They are comforting, thoughtful presences.
My bullmastiffs sat quietly nearby while I wrote this article, watching me type; at least once while composing, I found myself talking to them. In their silent, expressive, constantly watchful faces, I found something that made it easier for me to think and write. So if Milei is taking economic policy advice from his dogs, the results speak—or perhaps bark—for themselves.
The post Javier Milei's Pack of Giant Libertarian Dogs appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: D.C. Rejects Robotaxis To Protect Jobs
articles.content:
The D.C. Council has rejected a bill that would have allowed autonomous vehicles (A.V.s) to operate in the country's capital.
During a session of the D.C. Council's Committee on Transportation and the Environment on Thursday, the Autonomous Vehicle Deployment Authorization Amendment Act of 2026 was defeated in a 3–3 vote. Councilmember Charles Allen, who introduced the bill, Council Chair Phil Mendelson, and Christina Henderson, voted in favor. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George and Councilmembers Zachary Parker and Elissa Silverman voted against.
The legislation would have created the first legal pathway for companies to operate driverless taxis and delivery vehicles in the district, potentially preventing thousands of road accidents in the process. Waymo, an autonomous driving technology company, analyzed more than 271 million miles without a human driver. The results showed autonomous vehicles were involved in 95 percent fewer crashes resulting in serious injuries or fatalities, 93 percent fewer pedestrian injury crashes, and 86 percent fewer cyclist crashes with injuries compared with human drivers travelling comparable distances. In July, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety published research finding similar results—Waymo's driverless vehicles were involved in 68 percent fewer police-reportable crashes and 81 percent fewer injury crashes per mile than human drivers.
As Allen argued at Thursday's hearing, "A.V.s do not drive while impaired, distracted, or tired. They can be programmed to follow traffic laws that are all too often broken with deadly consequences."
Despite evidence that A.V.s could improve road safety, which was acknowledged, the bill failed primarily due to opposition from lawmakers concerned about the impact of automation on existing workers. "I support bringing autonomous vehicles to the district," said councilmember Parker, who voted against the legislation. "My concerns include impacts on existing jobs, and the degree to which new jobs or other benefits secured in this legislation will help individuals who stand to lose out."
Concessions were already made to lawmakers concerned about job displacement. The original bill would have imposed a costly regulatory framework, including an extraordinarily expensive $6 million three-year permit, $5 million in insurance, and a tax of 15 cents on every mile driven, in part to fund government training programs for rideshare drivers. Prior to Thursday's vote, the bill received a substantial rewrite to make even more concessions, including granting Uber and Lyft drivers collective bargaining rights, extending unionization rights to autonomous vehicle maintenance workers, and limiting the number of driverless vehicles to 200 per operator and 800 citywide. Yet even these concessions failed to win over politicians.
Parker expressed concern that autonomous vehicles would compete with unionized transportation services. "The bill also permits A.V.s with capacity up to 10 passengers," he said, "And I've heard from our friends in labor that they're concerned that that may decimate their union transit operations."
Arguing that automated vehicles, which may save lives, must be prohibited because they would compete with unionized labor is absurd. It also may not be true. A study published in Transportation Research Record found that public transit remained competitive with autonomous ridesharing services where good transit options were available. The researchers concluded that fears of a mass exodus from public transit to driverless vehicles may be limited, at least in the short term.
"My reference class for this kind of problem is infrastructure, where it's super common for people near a new infrastructure to say they don't want it," Lucas Pombo, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, tells Reason, while people who will benefit won't know that yet.
Technological progress has always disrupted existing industries. That doesn't mean we should try to stop it, particularly when the potential cost of doing so is measured in human lives.
The post D.C. Rejects Robotaxis To Protect Jobs appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Defamation Counterclaim Arising out Reagan National Helicopter Crash Case Can Go Forward
articles.content:
[A.] From Ellis v. Wallace, decided today by Chief Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak (D. Colo.):
On January 29, 2025, a Black Hawk Helicopter and American Airlines Flight 5342 collided mid-air near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Hours after the crash, several posts and articles appeared claiming Plaintiff was the helicopter pilot in the midair collision ("the rumor"), including:
- On the morning of January 30, 2025, a "well-known podcaster and influencer Luke Ford posted a full video identifying [Plaintiff] as the pilot and discussing the crash as intentional."
- On January 30, 2025, at 4:35 p.m., X user @RealNytoMwang posted "Plaintiff's photograph with text falsely identifying her as the transgender Black Hawk pilot who crashed the helicopter."
- On January 30, 2025, at 9:22 p.m., X user @FakeGayPolitics published a post "identifying Plaintiff as the pilot, including her photographs and video clips."
- On January 30, 2025, at 11:34 p.m., the Santa Monica Observer published an online article titled, "A Transgender Pilot Named Jo Ellis Flew Blackhawk Helicopter Into the American Airlines Jet at Reagan National."
Defendant made his first X post addressing the rumor on January 31, 2025, at 1:00 a.m. Eastern Time. And Plaintiff filed the Complaint in this matter on April 9, 2025, alleging that Defendant's posts were defamatory. Plaintiff then proceeded to appear as a guest on several podcasts. On July 18, 2025, she was interviewed on the Kill Tony podcast. During the interview, the hosts asked Plaintiff about the collision rumor and her pending litigation. Plaintiff explained that Defendant was the "[f]irst one to tie my likeness to the rumor. We don't know if he started the rumor, but he had millions of followers. He did the most what we can determine as damage."
Ten days later, Defendant filed the Special Motion to Dismiss Plaintiff's Complaint, attaching copies of X posts and articles linking Plaintiff to the crash hours before Defendant commented on the rumor. Plaintiff then appeared on a second podcast, the RVA Magazine podcast, on September 30, 2025. Plaintiff was again asked about the rumor and her pending litigation. In response, she stated:
[W]ithin 24 hours of the crash, I was finding out that I was being named as as the pilot as, like, the unnamed female pilot that was the supposed DEI hire that Trump, President Trump had alluded to at a press conference that "we know it's DEI because we just know." And so that kind of sent the online world into a frenzy of like, let's figure out who this pilot is. And, from what we can tell, [Defendant] picked up on that and used a picture of me and the [Michael] Smerconish article and, um, kind of put it all together. And with his following, he had, I think, two and half million followers or something like that, we believe he did the most damage. Like it would not have had the legs it had if he hadn't posted about it.
Finally, on January 12, 2026, Kim Congdon interviewed Plaintiff on The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast. Congdon asked Plaintiff if she was suing the individual that started the rumor. Plaintiff responded:
I don't, yeah, I don't know if he started it, but he definitely, like, he pushed it. He's the first one to tie my likeness to it. Yeah. His name's Matt Wallace and, uh, he, uh, millions of followers on Twitter, and he pushed it pretty hard and we believe he did the most damage and so I'm suing him in federal court."
On April 6, 2026, Defendant filed the Counterclaim alleging that these podcast statements were defamatory.
Defendant alleges that Plaintiff made repeated defamatory statements that: (1) Defendant "was the first one to post [Plaintiff's] likeness in connection with the helicopter crash," and (2) that Plaintiff believes Defendant's "statements caused the most damage." {Plaintiff alleges that there is a material difference between claiming that Defendant was the first to name Plaintiff in relation to the tragedy, and that Defendant was the first one to post Plaintiff's likeness in connection with the collision. The distinction is unclear to the Court. Accordingly, the Court assesses Plaintiff's "likeness" statements as conveying Defendant was the first to connect Plaintiff to the collision.}
[B.] The court rejected Plaintiff's arguments that Plaintiff's statements were protected by the "litigation privilege." That privilege bars defamation lawsuits based on statements in court filings and in-court statements, but doesn't apply to statements about the lawsuit made outside the litigation.
(Recall that, though in a typical case it would be a defendant who's arguing the statements were privileged, opinion, true, etc., and plaintiff would be responding, here the roles are flipped because the defendant is counterclaiming against plaintiff based on plaintiff's statements.)
[C.] The court also rejected Plaintiff's arguments that the statements were nonactionable opinion: It concluded that both statements were "susceptible of being proved true or false," and were framed as factual assertions rather than using "loose or hyperbolic language that provided the impression that her statements should not be taken seriously."
[D.] The court concluded that Defendant had introduced sufficient evidence that the statements were false:
First, with respect to Plaintiff's "likeness" statements, Plaintiff repeatedly claimed that Defendant was "the first one to tie [her] likeness to the rumor." However, Defendant provided several pieces of evidence showing that other X users linked Plaintiff to the rumor before Defendant….
Second, Defendant has shown a reasonable likelihood of proving by clear and convincing evidence that Plaintiff's "most damage" statements were false. Defendant declares that "the rumor was spread primarily by much larger voices than [Defendant's,] such as Ann Coulter's, Alex Jones's, and others." He claims that these "prominent individuals and entities" had a "far greater reach than anything [he] posted" about Plaintiff. If true, this declaration could provide clear and convincing evidence that Defendant's "most damage" statements were false. At the very least, it creates a question for the jury since Plaintiff has offered competing evidence. …
[E.] The court also concluded that Defendant had introduced sufficient evidence that Plaintiff knew the "likeness"/"first one to tie" statements were probably false (which is required by Colorado law in such cases):
First, Plaintiff's statements on the RVA Magazine podcast and The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast occurred after Defendant filed his Special Motion to Dismiss and Plaintiff filed her response. In his Special Motion to Dismiss, Defendant included evidence of other X users linking Plaintiff to the rumor before Defendant's first post. And Plaintiff's podcast statements referred to the ongoing litigation. Thus, it is plausible to infer that Plaintiff had a high degree of awareness of the probable falsity of her statements.
Second, Plaintiff's statements reveal inconsistencies in her account of the underlying events. During her interview on the Kill Tony podcast and The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast, Plaintiff repeatedly stated that she did not know whether Defendant started the rumor despite claiming he was "the first one to tie [her] likeness to it." Plaintiff repeated these conflicting statements in her declaration. was the first to blame [her] for this horrific crash because [she] clearly knew that information was incorrect.")] Consequently, such inconsistencies weigh in favor of finding that Defendant has shown a reasonable likelihood of proving actual malice by clear and convincing evidence….
But the court concluded there wasn't enough evidence of knowing or reckless falsehood as to the "most damage" statement:
Defendant declares that at the time Plaintiff made her public statements, she knew "prominent individuals and entities" had discussed her connection with the crash and that those individuals had a "far greater reach than anything [Defendant] posted." However, such evidence does not support an inference that Plaintiff entertained serious doubts as to the truth of the statements or was highly aware of their probable falsity. Further, Defendant provides no other evidence to support his actual malice claim here.
{A simple example demonstrates both this point and the distinction between Plaintiff's "likeness" statements. Assume five bloggers, each with five followers, each post about a famous actor having an affair. The affair did not occur. Subsequently, a podcaster with millions of followers posts that the actor was having an affair. Based upon this podcaster's broad following and reputation in the community, the New York Times—with significantly more subscribers than the podcaster—runs a story about the actor having an affair. If the actor states that the podcaster was the first to run the story, knowing five other bloggers ran the story, the actor spoke knowing her statement was false and thus acted with actual malice.
On the other hand, the mere fact that the actor stated that the podcaster did the most harm—even knowing the New York Times had a broader audience—does not necessarily equate to actual malice; the actor could easily believe (even if wrongfully) that the podcaster caused the most harm because the podcaster gave credibility to the false rumor and thus led others to run with the story. Here, Defendant has only presented evidence that those with broader audiences likewise posted the false story. But, as the hypothetical shows, this does not necessarily mean that Plaintiff's statement that Defendant caused the most damage was made with actual malice.}
[F.] Finally, the court concludes that Defendant had sufficiently alleged damages, as required by Colorado law:
Specifically, he alleged that Plaintiff's statements have caused: (1) "significant stress and strain in [his] family relations," and (2) stress from his alleged tarnished reputation. Although Plaintiff claims that that Defendant asserted these damages "in conclusory fashion," the Court finds the presented evidence sufficient to satisfy Defendant's burden at this stage.
The court thus denies Plaintiff's motion to dismiss as to the "likeness"/"first one to tie" statements, which means Defendant's counterclaim can go forward (though of course it doesn't mean the Defendant's counterclaim will ultimately prevail).
The post Defamation Counterclaim Arising out Reagan National Helicopter Crash Case Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason Magazine.

And Plaintiff's podcast statements referred to the ongoing litigation. Thus, it is plausible to infer that Plaintiff had a high degree of awareness of the probable falsity of her statements.

Second, Plaintiff's statements reveal inconsistencies in her account of the underlying events. During her interview on the Kill Tony podcast and The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast, Plaintiff repeatedly stated that she did not know whether Defendant started the rumor despite claiming he was "the first one to tie [her] likeness to it." Plaintiff repeated these conflicting statements in her declaration. was the first to blame [her] for this horrific crash because [she] clearly knew that information was incorrect.")] Consequently, such inconsistencies weigh in favor of finding that Defendant has shown a reasonable likelihood of proving actual malice by clear and convincing evidence….

But the court concluded there wasn't enough evidence of knowing or reckless falsehood as to the "most damage" statement:

Defendant declares that at the time Plaintiff made her public statements, she knew "prominent individuals and entities" had discussed her connection with the crash and that those individuals had a "far greater reach than anything [Defendant] posted." However, such evidence does not support an inference that Plaintiff entertained serious doubts as to the truth of the statements or was highly aware of their probable falsity. Further, Defendant provides no other evidence to support his actual malice claim here.

{A simple example demonstrates both this point and the distinction between Plaintiff's "likeness" statements. Assume five bloggers, each with five followers, each post about a famous actor having an affair. The affair did not occur. Subsequently, a podcaster with millions of followers posts that the actor was having an affair. Based upon this podcaster's broad following and reputation in the community, the New York Times—with significantly more subscribers than the podcaster—runs a story about the actor having an affair. If the actor states that the podcaster was the first to run the story, knowing five other bloggers ran the story, the actor spoke knowing her statement was false and thus acted with actual malice.

On the other hand, the mere fact that the actor stated that the podcaster did the most harm—even knowing the New York Times had a broader audience—does not necessarily equate to actual malice; the actor could easily believe (even if wrongfully) that the podcaster caused the most harm because the podcaster gave credibility to the false rumor and thus led others to run with the story. Here, Defendant has only presented evidence that those with broader audiences likewise posted the false story. But, as the hypothetical shows, this does not necessarily mean that Plaintiff's statement that Defendant caused the most damage was made with actual malice.}

[F.] Finally, the court concludes that Defendant had sufficiently alleged damages, as required by Colorado law:

Specifically, he alleged that Plaintiff's statements have caused: (1) "significant stress and strain in [his] family relations," and (2) stress from his alleged tarnished reputation. Although Plaintiff claims that that Defendant asserted these damages "in conclusory fashion," the Court finds the presented evidence sufficient to satisfy Defendant's burden at this stage.

The court thus denies Plaintiff's motion to dismiss as to the "likeness"/"first one to tie" statements, which means Defendant's counterclaim can go forward (though of course it doesn't mean the Defendant's counterclaim will ultimately prevail).

The post Defamation Counterclaim Arising out Reagan National Helicopter Crash Case Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Maine ICE Officer Who Killed a Man Had a Past Full of Red Flags
articles.content:
David Brouillette is the rookie Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot and killed Colombian migrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a traffic stop in July. Newly released messages show that the officer had it out for immigrants, particularly Colombians. This comes on the heels of reports that Brouillette had a sporadic job record and a history of domestic abuse allegations and mental illness. All of this raises the question: Just how much is ICE vetting its hires?
ICE agents tried to stop Durán Guerrero's car when they were staking out his Maine apartment in search of someone else. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed after the shooting that Durán Guerrero "attempted to flee the scene" in his vehicle and that Brouillette then fired out of fear for public safety. Lawyers for Durán Guerrero's family have said that he had a valid work authorization to be in the U.S. and had no criminal record. There is no bodycam footage, and the incident is still under investigation.
Now The New York Times has obtained a series of angry emails that Brouillette wrote to his sister about her longtime boyfriend and father of her children, a man of Colombian descent. Among other things, Brouillette said that her partner "can take his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries," that his "bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers," and that "Your choices have cost you a brother. I am so so so ashamed of you. You're dead to me Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me. DEAD."
Those messages—a snapshot, his sister said, of his anger toward people born outside the United States—are not the only eyebrow-raising element of Brouillette's history to emerge since the shooting. According to the Associated Press, a family member claims he was diagnosed with severe bipolar and attention deficit disorder when he was a child. His sister, a licensed therapist, says his condition worsened since he returned from service in Afghanistan in 2013 and that he has been struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder.
Brouillette's mother told the Times that her son "is dangerous and should not have weapons." (She also said: "Believe his victims, not him.") His two former wives have both claimed that he had physically abused them, which he has disputed. His daughter told the Associated Press that he said to her after school one day that he had been sitting on a tree stump with a gun to his head.
Brouillette bounced between at least half a dozen jobs from 2015 to 2025. He had a short stint as a volunteer firefighter in late 2021; the then–fire chief has called him "a loose cannon," saying, "It didn't take me long to recognize that I'd made a mistake."
He suffered a traumatic brain injury during a firefighter training exercise at Southern Maine Community College. He sued the school two years later in 2023, claiming that the injury caused lasting symptoms including "impaired memory, cognitive deficits, headaches, vertigo and light sensitivity."
"He was a walking red flag," says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. "He should not have been allowed within a mile of a law enforcement job…and yet ICE not only brought him on board, but they fast-tracked him into the field."
Brouillette was hired in December amid the Trump administration's effort to bolster ICE's numbers. According to the Times, the agency allowed him to skip parts of the full training program as part of its more relaxed protocols for former law enforcement officers. On the day of the shooting, his background check was still incomplete.
When CNN asked border czar Tom Homan about Brouillette, Homan called him a "rare instance." But David J. Bier, director of Immigration Studies at the Cato Institute, argues that even if that's true, just a few "rare instances" can have an enormous impact. "One is too many," Bier tells Reason. "When you say it's just a few people, well, those few people are interacting with thousands of people every year. So it really doesn't take many mistakes in the hiring process to have really big implications for the perception of ICE and the impact on the public."
"The worrying thing is we don't know how many other people out there are like him," Reichlin-Melnick tells Reason. Some reports suggest that ICE has been quietly sacking recruits, uncovering problems in their backgrounds after the fact. A former federal official from the agency told the Times that hundreds hired during the surge had already been removed; a recent Washington Post report uncovered 19 officers with past allegations of misconduct, criminal charges, or other employment red flags.
A 17-year ICE employee who oversaw the vetting process filed a formal whistleblower's complaint with the DHS Office of Inspector General in August 2025. The complaint says that "systemic breakdowns in vetting" have led to people getting job offers before even basic preliminary vetting, such as identity verification and credit checks. It also states that the DHS engaged in "deliberate circumvention of personnel vetting and clearance procedures in violation of governing law and policy," and it calls for an immediate halt of job offers until proper standards had been restored.
The DHS didn't heed his warning. Brouillette was brought on three months later. Seven months after that, Durán Guerrero was dead.
The post Maine ICE Officer Who Killed a Man Had a Past Full of Red Flags appeared first on Reason Magazine.
